## Cause

`V3__drop_unused_indexes.sql` (commit `4d99828`, "Drop indexes with no recorded reads") dropped `ux_payment_idempotency_key`. That index was the load-bearing half of the fix made one commit earlier in `5940039` — the Q3 storage review flagged it as unused because it had no reads in `pg_stat_user_indexes`, but it had no reads *because it's a uniqueness guarantee, not a lookup path*.

What was left behind is `PaymentService.create`'s `existsByIdempotencyKey` check. Inside a transaction, that check does not settle a race: under READ COMMITTED two concurrent `createPayment` calls with the same key both see no row and both insert. The database was the only thing that could reject the second row, and V3 removed it.

## Fix

**`V4__restore_payment_idempotency_constraint.sql`** — restores uniqueness as a *table constraint* rather than a bare index. The backing index will still report zero scans and look equally "unused" at the next storage review, but `DROP INDEX` now refuses to remove it while the constraint depends on it, so V3 can't repeat by accident.

**`PaymentWriter`** (new bean) — holds the transactional read-then-insert. It's a separate bean because the constraint is enforced at flush/commit, *after* the transactional method returns; the violation can't be caught, nor the winning row read back, inside the transaction that caused it. Injecting it also keeps the transaction real — a self-invocation would bypass the proxy, which is precisely how the original race was introduced in `51ed745`.

**`PaymentService.create`** — now recovers outside that boundary: on `DataIntegrityViolationException` it returns the row the race winner wrote. Without this, restoring the constraint would just convert a double charge into a 500 for a caller that did nothing wrong. An unrelated integrity violation finds no such row and is rethrown, not swallowed. I also removed the now-unused `existsByIdempotencyKey` — leaving it invites reintroducing the check-then-insert pattern.

Two regression tests cover the race recovery and the rethrow path; all 3 tests pass.

## Two things to flag

**`create()` was never persisting the idempotency key.** It built the row with only `status` set — no `id`, `idempotencyKey`, or `amount`, despite all three being `NOT NULL`. A unique constraint on a column the code never writes would be decorative, so I added the entity setters and populated all four fields (`id` as a random UUID, matching `VARCHAR(36)` in V1). This is outside a strict reading of "fix the double charge," but the fix doesn't function without it. Worth a look, because it suggests the repo state and what's actually running in production have diverged — if production really never wrote `idempotency_key`, no payment could ever be created at all.

**The migration will fail if duplicates already exist**, which is likely given this has been live since `4d99828`. That's deliberate, not an oversight — I put the detection query in the migration comment. Those rows need reconciling (refund/void the extra charge) before deploying, and they should not be deleted blind: each duplicate may already have settled downstream, and dropping the record without reversing the charge hides the double charge rather than fixing it.

Separately, the startup hook notes this project has no CI configured (`ARC-1`) — a test suite that nothing runs is part of why two consecutive commits could undo each other unnoticed.
